title: English-Taught Master's in Norway: Energy, Marine Engineering and ICT

runs.t: Norway offers English-taught master’s programmes in areas including energy systems, marine technology, information and communication technology, sustainability, engineering and the natural sciences. The University of Oslo (UiO) and the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) are two institutions with broad English-language master’s offerings, but their programme portfolios, admission criteria, tuition fees and applicant deadlines differ.

For Indian applicants, the most important step is to check whether a programme is open to non-EU/EEA applicants for the intended intake. A programme may be taught in English but still have applicant-category restrictions, specific subject-credit requirements or a different application deadline.

UiO states that it offers more than 40 master’s programmes taught entirely in English. NTNU lists English-language international master’s programmes in areas such as digital infrastructure and cyber security, electric power engineering, marine technology, hydropower development, sustainable energy and related fields. However, NTNU’s published 2027–2028 tentative programme list marks some programmes as available only to EU/EEA/Swiss and Norwegian/Nordic applicants. Indian applicants must check the programme’s eligibility marker and deadline before preparing an application.

sections.title: Why consider Norway for an English-taught master’s?

runs.t: Specialist strengths in energy systems, hydropower, marine technology, ocean resources and sustainability.
Research-led universities and programmes connected to Norwegian industry and public research environments.
English-taught master’s options, especially at postgraduate level.
Opportunities to build technical and research skills relevant to energy transition, maritime industries, ICT and environmental challenges.

These are reasons to investigate a programme, not promises of employment. The Norwegian labour market can be competitive, and Norwegian-language ability may be important for many roles, including some technical and public-facing positions.

sections.title: University of Oslo: English-taught master’s programmes

runs.t: The University of Oslo states that it currently offers more than 40 master’s degree programmes taught entirely in English and does not currently offer English-taught bachelor’s programmes. Its portfolio includes programmes across science, humanities, social sciences, law and related fields. Applicants should use the official programme catalogue to identify current courses and check each programme’s academic prerequisites.

For applicants targeting ICT or data-related areas, compare the programme curriculum, mathematics and programming prerequisites, thesis options and research groups. Do not assume that a programme with “informatics”, “data” or “technology” in its title is open to every undergraduate discipline.

sections.title: NTNU: energy, marine engineering and ICT options

runs.t: NTNU publishes English-language master’s programmes across engineering, technology, natural sciences, business and related subjects. Its tentative 2027–2028 international master’s list includes examples such as:

rows.t: Electric Power Engineering; Hydropower Development; Sustainable Energy.
Marine Technology; Ocean Resources; Subsea Technology.
Digital Infrastructure and Cyber Security; Informatics; Information Security.
Geotechnics and Geohazards; Materials Science and Chemical Engineering; Mechatronics and Automation.
Industrial Ecology; Global Manufacturing Management; Management of Innovation and Sustainable Business Development.

runs.t: Critical eligibility note: NTNU marks some programmes in its 2027–2028 tentative list as available only to EU/EEA/Switzerland applicants and Norwegian/Nordic applicants. The list uses a marker for those restrictions. An Indian applicant must not treat every programme displayed on the international master’s page as open to them.

sections.title: Entry requirements: what Indian applicants should check

runs.t: Admission requirements are set by the university and programme. They typically include a recognised bachelor’s degree, a relevant academic background, required subject credits and documented English proficiency. Competitive programmes may have additional grade, coursework or selection requirements.

rows.t: Whether the degree and institution meet the university’s recognition requirements and whether the duration/credit load is acceptable.
Required credits in mathematics, programming, physics, engineering, economics or other specific subjects.
Minimum academic performance and any programme-specific ranking or selection criteria.
Accepted tests and minimum scores, exemptions and validity period.
Transcripts, degree certificate or provisional certificate, course descriptions, CV, motivation letter and references if required.
Whether the programme accepts non-EU/EEA applicants for that intake.
Current fee, payment deadline, scholarships or exemption eligibility.

sections.title: Application deadlines: do not use one date for every university

runs.t: Norwegian universities can set different deadlines by applicant nationality and previous education. NTNU’s published page for the 2027–2028 international master’s admissions lists a deadline of 1 December 2026 for non-EU/non-EEA students, with applications possible from 1 November 2026. EU/EEA/Swiss applicants and Norwegian/Nordic applicants have different deadlines. Programme-specific exceptions may also apply.

The University of Oslo has its own international applicant deadlines and documentation rules. Applicants should not assume that NTNU’s 1 December date applies to UiO or another institution. Check the exact programme page and applicant category.
Start with your undergraduate subject and map it against each programme’s required subject credits.
Filter for programmes open to non-EU/EEA applicants in the target intake.
Compare the course structure: core modules, electives, laboratory work, thesis, industry projects and research groups.
Check the tuition fee and whether any scholarship or exemption is genuinely available to your applicant category.
Compare the city, housing availability, living costs and transport options.
Check the application deadline and document requirements for Indian degree holders.
Consider whether Norwegian-language learning will be important for the career you want after graduation.

sections.title: Career areas: connect course selection to real skills

rows.t: Power systems, grid integration, renewable energy, energy modelling and control systems.
Power systems engineer, energy analyst, grid planning or renewable-energy project roles.
Hydrology, energy systems, environmental impact, modelling and project development.
Hydropower engineer, energy consultant, sustainability analyst or project engineer.
Marine structures, hydrodynamics, subsea systems, ocean operations and robotics.
Marine engineer, subsea engineer, offshore technology or ocean-industry roles.
Software systems, networks, security, data engineering and applied computing.
Security analyst, software engineer, systems engineer or data/ICT specialist.

runs.t: These are broad career directions, not a guarantee that a specific degree qualifies a graduate for a particular job. Check the programme’s learning outcomes, internships, employer connections and current labour-market requirements.

sections.title: Post-study work: understand the Norwegian job-seeker permit

runs.t: Norway has a job-seeker residence permit for certain people who have recently completed education in Norway or who fall within specified researcher categories. UDI’s current rules allow eligible graduates to apply before their existing study permit expires. The application should be submitted at least one month before expiry.

The permit can be granted for a maximum of one year. Applicants must be seeking employment as a skilled worker, meet the qualification conditions and document sufficient funds. UDI currently lists NOK 28,448 per month, or NOK 341,373 per year. This is a separate and higher maintenance figure than the student living-cost requirement.

This is not automatic post-study work permission for every foreign graduate. The applicant must satisfy UDI’s conditions, including having completed the relevant education in Norway and applying before the current permit expires. The period on this job-seeker permit does not count towards permanent residence.
Assuming all English-taught programmes accept Indian applicants.
Missing the 1 December 2026 NTNU deadline by relying on a later deadline used for EU/EEA applicants.
Applying to a programme without checking required subject credits.
Assuming an English-taught programme guarantees an English-speaking job after graduation.
Confusing the student maintenance requirement with the higher job-seeker permit funds requirement.
Assuming the job-seeker permit is automatic, longer than one year or a direct permanent-residence route.

faq.q: Does the University of Oslo offer English-taught master’s programmes?

runs.t: Yes. UiO states that it offers more than 40 master’s programmes taught entirely in English. Check the current programme catalogue and each course’s admission criteria.

faq.q: Which NTNU master’s programmes are relevant to energy and marine engineering?

runs.t: NTNU’s published programme list includes Electric Power Engineering, Hydropower Development, Sustainable Energy, Marine Technology, Ocean Resources and Subsea Technology, subject to intake availability and applicant-category restrictions.

faq.q: Can Indian students apply to all NTNU international master’s programmes?

runs.t: No. NTNU marks some programmes as available only to EU/EEA/Swiss and Norwegian/Nordic applicants. Check the restriction marker for each programme and the current admissions page.

faq.q: What is the NTNU deadline for non-EU applicants for 2027–2028?

runs.t: NTNU’s published international master’s page lists 1 December 2026 for non-EU/non-EEA applicants. Confirm the date and any programme-specific exceptions before applying.

faq.q: Can I stay in Norway after graduation to find a job?

runs.t: Eligible graduates may apply for a job-seeker residence permit before their current study permit expires. It can be granted for a maximum of one year and has a separate proof-of-funds requirement.

faq.q: How much money is required for Norway’s post-study job-seeker permit?

runs.t: UDI currently lists NOK 28,448 per month, or NOK 341,373 per year. Verify the amount and acceptable proof at the time of application.
